newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bourse leaps further as foreigners rush in.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse leaps further as foreigners rush in.

text.p: The Thai stock market soared for the second consecutive day on Thursday as foreign investors led the rush to buy stocks sparked by the decision to float the baht.
The key index of the Stock Exchange of Thailand closed nearly nine percent up, gaining 49.19 points to 617.98, in brisk trade with about 8.7 billion baht of shares changing hands.
"I think it's a vote of confidence that the Bank of Thailand finally realised we've got a problem," said Graham Catterwell, head of equities for Morgan Grenfell.

The bourse, which was mired in eight-year lows for most of the past two months, has gained more than 90 points, or around 17 percent, in the past two days. It is now at a level not seen since early May.
"This is amazing," said a foreign analyst. "There has been a lot of panic buying. When people pile in they really want in and don't care. There are still a lot of orders coming in from overseas."
Most analysts were reluctant to make forecasts, but some said they thought the rally would be capped at an index level of around 650.
The government's move to float the baht and drop a 13-year old policy of pegging it to a basket of currencies was the latest in a series of measures to help Thailand's ailing economy.
The baht, which lost about 15-20 percent of its value after the government announced the managed float, was relatively steady at levels seen late on Wednesday.
It was quoted at around 29.00/29.50 bid/ask offshore and 28.25/28.65 in local markets at around 1000 GMT.
This compares with its new baht/dollar reference rate of 27.383 set by the Bank of Thailand early on Thursday.
The rate, which is a weighted average of traded levels on Wednesday, is about six percent weaker than the 25.85 onshore baht level seen before news of the managed float.
Analysts said it was a bit firm, but with capital controls still in place, onshore and offshore rates were likely to converge over time.
Others predicted the baht would hover at around 28-29 to the dollar for the rest of the year, provided there were no fresh shocks to the economy.
The currency was quiet in late trade, with many investors still trying to digest and understand the new exchange rate system, which they called a de facto devaluation.
Analysts said equity investors were taking little notice of slight fluctuations in the baht or the reference rate now, as many felt most of the currency's slide was over.

"The big hit has already been taken," said one foreign analyst. "But people who are coming in to buy aren't really worried. The market is going up so fast they'll more than recoup any exchange losses."
Some analysts warned that foreign board share prices might have jumped too high and there may be a need for consolidation soon.
Although the short-term market forecast might be rosy and investors were buying blue-chip stocks across the board, Thailand's economy was not yet out of the woods, they said.
"The game is not over yet," said Catterwell. "They still have to work out problems with the finance and property sectors. There's still work to do."
